subtype: Approach: trying to memorise everything in the encyclopedia [Pitfall]
passage: Three weeks before the inter-school quiz, Vaibhav walked into the school library and asked Jahnavi ma'am for the thickest encyclopaedia. "I'm going to learn all of it." By the second week his eyes hurt, he had forgotten most of A, and he still didn't know whether the quiz even had animal questions. On Friday he closed the book with a thump and put his head on it. Jahnavi ma'am came over quietly. "Shall we find out what the quiz actually asks?"

I watched him from the other bed. Every night he read under the table lamp, lips moving. The first week he was excited and kept telling me facts at breakfast. The second week he stopped telling me facts. The third week he fell asleep on page two hundred with the light on. When our cousin Ramesh tested him with an old quiz sheet, Chetan got seven out of thirty. He stared at the sheet. "I read all of this," he said. "Where did it go?" I don't know what he felt exactly. He didn't open the book the next night.

subtype: Approach: practising with a partner using mock rounds [Action]
passage: Omkar, you want to know how your Lalit Dada won the Class 5 quiz? Not with luck. My friend Joseph and I made a plan. We couldn't buy a buzzer, so we used my mother's steel spoons and the thali. Every evening for two weeks, my father sat on the charpai with the question book and read, and we banged the thali when we knew. Whoever banged first answered. Oh, the noise! The neighbours complained. But by the third evening we knew something. Joseph was quicker on science. I was quicker on cricket. And both of us were hopeless on world capitals. So we spent the last week on capitals only. In the final, the last question was a capital. We banged together.

The next day Bhavna came over with an atlas from the school library, and they pinned my old world map above the dining table. For a week, every evening, I heard them quizzing each other: "Nairobi!" "Yangtze!" On the next Sunday I read a new set. They missed only one geography question.

subtype: Approach: deciding when to guess and when to pass [Thinking]
passage: Before the quiz, Ayesha Miss explained the rules. In the pass round, a right answer gets ten points, but a wrong answer loses five. I did the maths in my head. If I guessed and was wrong, I'd lose points we had already won. So I made a rule for myself: only buzz when I'm fairly sure, like I can see the answer. Otherwise, pass. My little sister, who came to watch, said, "Aadhya didi, you're passing so much!" I passed four questions. But I got seven right and none wrong. Our team came second, and the team that came fifth had guessed nearly every question. I still think about the ones I passed, but I don't regret it.

qa.q: How many points does a wrong answer lose in the pass round?
qa.a: A wrong answer loses five points.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel about passing so many questions?
qa.a: Aadhya felt calm and sure about the choice, even if the passed questions still come to mind now and then.

qa.q: What else could Aadhya do next time to be sure of more answers?
qa.a: Aadhya could study the topics she passed on, so more answers become fairly sure next time.

qa.q: How does Aadhya's passing look to her little sister?
qa.a: Her little sister finds it strange and says so, probably thinking a good player should answer everything.

grounding: It shows a girl learning that wrong answers lose points in the pass round and deciding to answer only when fairly sure.

Quiz coach's note, after Saturday's practice
Rukmini asked me before the round how the pass round works. I explained: plus ten for right, minus five for wrong. She thought for a moment and said, "So if I'm not sure, I should pass. Guessing costs." During practice she answered six questions, all correct, and passed on three. Two of her teammates guessed on almost everything and lost fifteen points between them. Afterwards Rukmini explained her thinking to them, a little shyly. I have asked her to share her "fairly sure" rule at Monday's team meeting, and I have added a column for passes on our score sheet so we can see how well each person judges.
- Pradeep, quiz coach

Varun is one of our quickest boys, and he loves the buzzer. Today he pressed it on five questions before I had finished reading them. "Which planet is closest to the sun, and which" - buzz - "Mercury!" The question was about the planet with the most moons. He got four of those five wrong and lost twenty points. He was frustrated and said the questions were tricky. I explained that quiz questions often turn at the end. We practised a rule: wait until the question mark, count one, then buzz. In the last ten questions he waited, got three right, and made no mistakes. I will keep reminding him.
- Lalit

"Salma, we keep answering over each other."

"Because you always look at me!"

"Science. And maths, sort of."
"I'm better at history and sports."

"And if I'm sure about a history one?"
"Then you whisper it to me, and I say it."
Lavanya held out her little finger. "Deal?"
"Deal."
In the next practice they didn't clash once.

subtype: Approach: dividing subjects between two teammates [Action]
passage: When Zeenat and I first practised for the inter-school quiz, it was a mess. We both knew some answers and both started talking at once, and the quiz master took our points away for two answers. So on the bus home, I took out my notebook and wrote two columns. Zeenat: history, sports, films. Vidya: science, maths, animals. General knowledge: whoever is sure, but the other one nods first. We read our columns every evening and only studied our own subjects. On the day we didn't clash once. In the science round Zeenat just sat back and smiled. It was strange, trusting someone else with half the answers, but it worked.

passage: In the Class 5 science club, Manoj sir gave everyone a blank page. "Write ten things you wonder about." Minakshi wrote fast: Do plants grow towards light? Why do cats purr? Sky: too hard. Music: she had no speaker. Ants: maybe, but ants run away. Light: two pots, a window and a cupboard, all at home. She had four weeks. She circled question one. subtype: Approach: planning a simple experiment with a fair test [Thinking]

Monday: Pranav wanted to know if beans need light. He took two plastic cups from the kitchen. "One goes on the windowsill," he told his sister Himani. "One goes in the dark cupboard." "And that's it?" "No. If one cup has more soil or more water, I won't know what made the difference."
Tuesday: He measured two spoons of soil into each cup, three beans in each, and marked a water line with a pen. "Same cup, same soil, same water. Only the light changes."
The next Monday: Both cups had sprouts. The windowsill ones were green and short; the cupboard ones were tall and yellow. "So the light did it," Pranav said. "Nothing else was different."

qa.q: How many beans did Pranav put in each cup?
qa.a: He put three beans in each cup.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when he said the light did it?
qa.a: He felt satisfied and sure, because he had kept everything else the same.

qa.q: What else could Pranav do to make his result stronger?
qa.a: He could repeat the test with more cups, so one odd bean doesn't decide the result.

qa.q: How does the experiment look to Himani?
qa.a: Himani first thinks it is just two cups, then sees how careful it is and can follow why the light made the difference.

subtype: Approach: planning a simple experiment with a fair test [Thinking]
passage: Saurabh, you're making a science project? Let your Bhupen Dada tell you about mine. When I was in Class 6, I wanted to prove that bean plants needed sunlight. My first idea was: one plant on the roof, one plant in a dark room. Easy. But my teacher asked, "Is the pot the same? The soil? The water?" I thought about it and realised I was using a big clay pot for one and a tiny tin for the other. If one grew better, how would I know why? So I found two identical tins, filled each with the same soil, gave each the same half glass of water every day. Only the light was different. After a week, the difference was clear, and I could explain it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Switching to two identical tins with the same soil and water mattered, because it made light the only difference.

qa.q: How might Bhupen's teacher have seen the final project?
qa.a: The teacher would likely be pleased that the question made Bhupen rethink and produce a fair test.

grounding: An elder recalls planning a bean experiment as a boy and making it fair by keeping pots, soil and water the same.
